projects.name: trainproof
projects.tagline: A deterministic linter for ML training runs.
projects.description: Deterministic PASS/WARN/FAIL verdicts across a training run's whole life — before it starts (dataset, tokenizer, and an environment preflight that catches a stack which will not import, an unreadable checkpoint, or too little system RAM), a live guardian during training, a post-run autopsy after, and a baseline compare. Reads five log formats including TensorBoard event files, decoded from the wire format with no torch, tensorflow or tensorboard installed. No ML judging ML: every verdict is a rule that fires or doesn't, every finding cites its exact numbers, and a check that could not run is reported as NOT-CHECKED rather than as a pass.
projects._note: Mechanical fields (version, date, release_count, tests_passing) are written by gen_site_data.py from GitHub Releases, PyPI and pytest --collect-only; release titles and summaries are authored by hand because that producer refuses to invent prose. GitHub Releases and PyPI agree at 12 releases. v0.12.0 uploaded to PyPI 2026-07-31. Verified 2026-07-31.
highlights: Objective checks: catches a cross-entropy ignore_index that is also a valid output class - a collision that silently deletes a target from the loss while leaving the loss curve indistinguishable from a correct run (0.0035 vs 0.0034)
trainproof doctor . — zero-config autopsy: discovers every training log in a directory, judges them, prints a triage-sorted summary
Live guardian: a one-line Hugging Face callback; opt-in stop_on_fail aborted a diverging Qwen2.5-3B QLoRA at step 20 of 300 in a real demo
Preflight: lints dataset + tokenizer before a single GPU-second (malformed JSONL, empty rows, duplicates, missing eos/pad, over-length)
compare catches shuffled-labels corruption that single-run loss rules cannot — the relative loss floor sits ~6× a known-good baseline
Stable rule IDs (TP-DIVERGE, TP-OVERFIT, TP-DEAD-RUN, …) documented in RULES.md, plus --json output built for CI and AI coding agents
CONTRACTS.md pins the promises — exit codes, JSON schema policy, rule-ID stability and a verdict-stability guarantee; SARIF 2.1.0 output turns findings into GitHub PR annotations
A PASS names every check that ran and every check it skipped, with the reason — a skipped check is never reported as a passed one

Grounded in an 18-run fault-injection study (Qwen2.5-3B QLoRA, RTX 5080) — six configurations at three seeds each, every real log shipped in-repo — plus a 9.8-hour Coqui XTTS fine-tune that diverged on its own, the first shipped failure nobody injected

Reads five log formats including TensorBoard event files, decoded from the wire format with no tensorflow, tensorboard, protobuf, torch or numpy — validated byte-exact against tensorboard's own EventAccumulator, and the rules are exercised on real runs from three frameworks: HuggingFace, Coqui XTTS and PyTorch Lightning

releases.title: 0.18.1 — the core no longer drags in an audio stack
releases.summary: No rule, threshold or verdict changed. numpy, soundfile and ttsproof were hard runtime dependencies used by exactly one module — the speech dataset check — which cli.py imported at module scope. So `pip install trainproof` pulled an audio stack, and `trainproof epoch` on a text log would not start without libsndfile, the C library behind soundfile. For a tool whose tfevents reader is written from the wire format specifically to avoid installing TensorFlow, that was the wrong shape. `dependencies` is now empty; the three moved to a `trainproof[speech]` extra, the speech check resolves lazily through a module __getattr__, and cli.py imports it inside the `data` subcommand. A core install that calls a speech check without the extra gets a legible error naming `pip install 'trainproof[speech]'`, not a bare ImportError. Sixteen new tests block all three packages at the import system in a fresh interpreter and assert that twelve core modules and the `epoch` CLI still work, so a stray top-level import cannot quietly reintroduce the coupling. 258 -> 274 tests.

releases.title: v0.18.0 - the objective release
releases.summary: Every rule until now read the training run: the loss curve, the gradient norms, the learning rate. This release adds the first rules that read the OBJECTIVE - the output layer, the ignore sentinel, and which classes actually reach the loss as positive targets. TP-OBJ-IGNORE-INDEX-COLLISION fires when a cross-entropy ignore_index is a valid class in the output layer, so every target carrying that id is discarded before the loss and can never be learned. TP-OBJ-DEAD-CLASS fires when a class exists in the output layer but never once appears as a positive target while coverage of the others is broad. Both are decidable at step 0 and are deliberately independent of the curve, because the failure that motivated them is invisible to it: a minimal reproduction with the collision and without it ends at 0.0035 and 0.0034 final loss - indistinguishable, while the broken arm assigns the stop token a probability of 0.000001 and never terminates and the fixed arm assigns 0.996565 and terminates every time. The Hugging Face callback runs both once in on_train_begin, before step 1, inferring the output-layer width and the sentinel from the model and sampling the first batches of labels - no new call site, no user action, and under stop_on_fail a broken objective aborts the run before a GPU-second is spent. 84 -> 90 rule IDs, no existing rule, threshold or verdict changed. 245 -> 258 tests.

releases.title: v0.17.0 — the lint gate, and one log that used to vanish
v0.16.0 — the rule registry (no behaviour change)
The third-framework release
releases.summary: Every rule shipped so far had only ever been tested against HuggingFace trainer_state.json. PyTorch Lightning, Fish Speech and most research code write their metrics to TensorBoard event files and nowhere else, so those runs were invisible — a Lightning run could overfit for three hours and trainproof had nothing to read. Adds a fifth log format, tfevents, written from the wire format (TFRecord framing plus the Event, Summary and TensorProto fields required). It imports no tensorflow, no tensorboard, no protobuf, no torch and no numpy: reading a log file should not require installing a training stack. Validated against the reference implementation rather than against itself — on a real 2049-step Lightning run it reproduces tensorboard's own EventAccumulator byte-exact, all 13 tags, every point count, values to 1e-6. Rank-0 tensor scalars are decoded alongside simple_value, because Lightning writes the former and a reader handling only the latter sees an empty run. Tag normalisation resolves train/loss, TrainIterStats/loss and training/loss to one column; when several tags claim a column the denser series wins, ties alphabetical, so selection is deterministic. Truncated files — the normal state of a killed run — are read up to the cut. Fixes a TP-ZERO-GRAD false positive found by running the shipped rules against a real run rather than by a test: the rule condemned any run whose finite gradient norms were all exactly 0.0, and Coqui writes avg_grad_norm as 0.0 when clipping is off, so a healthy 125,000-step XTTS fine-tune that reached loss 0.017 was reported FAIL. A run cannot both learn and receive no gradient, so the check now stands down when the loss improved and stays armed when it did not. evidence/ ships the logs behind the claims: a 125,000-step Coqui XTTS v2 fine-tune as both a text log and the event file from the same run — parsed by independent readers, agreeing exactly, an agreement EVIDENCE_MATRIX now computes rather than asserts — and a 2049-step Fish Speech LoRA fine-tune whose eval loss bottomed out at step 99 and climbed to 16.19 while train loss kept falling. No new rule IDs (62) and no schema change (schema_version 3). 179 → 210 tests.

releases.title: The third-state release
releases.summary: A log that carried a loss column but executed zero check groups returned PASS with exit 0. "Checked and clean" and "nothing could be checked" shared one verdict and one exit code, which is the only surface CI reads. This release separates them. New verdict NOT-CHECKED and rule TP-NOT-CHECKED, emitted when zero check groups execute — in practice a short run with fewer than five finite loss points and a non-positive mean loss, the sub-threshold companion to TP-ZERO-LOSS. Its message states how many groups were considered and carries the skip reason for every one of them. Severity and exit code became two explicit axes: severity orders FAIL, WARN, NOT-CHECKED, PASS, while the exit code is 1 if anything failed, 2 if anything could not be judged, 0 otherwise. An unrecognised verdict now normalises to NOT-CHECKED instead of falling through as a pass, so the enum stays closed. The release also shipped with a defect caught in review before publication: the console renderer had no NOT-CHECKED branch and printed the new verdict as [FAIL] — a release designed to stop a false PASS would have shipped a false FAIL. schema_version 2 → 3, since the verdict enum gained a member. 171 → 179 tests.

releases.title: The honest-verdict release
releases.summary: No new diagnostic idea — every change closes a hole in a check that already existed. An audit asked what happens to a run whose loss is exactly 0.0 on every step, and the answer was: every loss-shape check skips, because each is guarded against dividing by zero, the verdict stays PASS, and the PASS then names those same three checks as having run. A run that learned nothing passed, and was told which checks had cleared it. New rules: TP-ZERO-LOSS and TP-ZERO-GRAD name the two degenerate series (all labels masked to -100; a severed backward graph, which was previously misdiagnosed as a dead run). TP-CMP-UNCOMPARABLE stops compare reporting a zero-loss run as favorable — a zero loss floor beats any baseline. TP-CMP-ERROR replaces a silent exception swallow in doctor --baseline. TP-PASS now reports only checks that actually executed, each skip with its reason, exposed as a structured checks key. TP-DIVERGE took its floor over all losses, so one 0.0 anywhere disabled divergence detection for a whole run. The Hugging Face callback had been dropping every eval entry, making TP-OVERFIT structurally unreachable there. Six threshold values in RULES.md disagreed with the code. 116 → 166 tests; all 38 golden snapshots byte-identical, so no existing verdict changed.

releases.title: The evidence release
releases.summary: No rule and no threshold changed — every verdict from 0.10.0 is byte-identical in tests/golden/. What changed is how much evidence ships, and whether the documents describing it can drift from the data. All three seeds of every gallery configuration now ship: 18 runs, six configurations at seeds 42/43/44, where previously only one seed per configuration was committed — so "three seeds out of three" became a claim a reader can check. New: examples/real_world/xtts_diverged, a 9.8-hour Coqui XTTS fine-tune that diverged on its own, the first shipped failure nobody injected and the only Coqui-format fixture. EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md is now generated from the logs by scripts/regenerate_evidence.py, version-stamped and carrying the rule IDs that fired in each cell, with a test that fails the build if it goes stale — it had been publishing v0.3-dev verdicts against a v0.10 engine. python -m trainproof now works. The HTML report became opt-in via epoch --html instead of being written into the caller's working directory on every run. 116 tests.

releases.title: The contract release
releases.summary: Nothing about how trainproof judges a run changed — no rule, no threshold, no verdict moved, and every gallery verdict is now locked byte-identical in tests/golden/. What changed is what trainproof promises, written down in CONTRACTS.md: exit codes, JSON schema policy, rule-ID stability, SARIF mapping, and the pre-1.0 breaking-change policy. Adds SARIF 2.1.0 output (--sarif) so findings become GitHub PR annotations, and --json on data/tokenizer/preflight. BREAKING: exit code 2 now means "trainproof could not judge" (unreadable logs, missing files, missing optional deps), separating tool errors from a FAIL verdict about your run; schema_version is now 2, with doctor merging compare findings into one findings array tagged by source. Fixes a real bug: doctor --baseline printed [FAIL] comparisons but still exited 0.

releases.title: The eval-aware release
releases.summary: Reads the eval curve. New TP-OVERFIT (WARN): eval_loss rising past 1.2× its own minimum while train_loss keeps falling (needs ≥ 4 eval points). Fixed a false TP-DIVERGE caused by HF's training-summary entry (a run-average train_loss) leaking into the per-step loss series. Grounded in a real Qwen2.5-3B QLoRA overfit run now in examples/gallery/overfit. 57 tests.

releases.title: The trust release
releases.summary: Canonical record contract — adapters are the only place columns map to canonical keys, exact-name matching (eval_loss can no longer be mistaken for training loss). Stable rule IDs documented in RULES.md. Honest PASS names which check groups ran and which were skipped. Machine-readable --json. BREAKING for text-parsers: output lines now carry the rule ID — parse --json. 52 tests.

releases.title: Guardian telemetry
releases.summary: Live step-time telemetry via TrainproofCallback. New deterministic timing rules that fire only when timing fields exist: step-time cliff (WARN) and dataloader-bound (WARN). Stall heartbeat: watch --stall-timeout warns once per stall episode when the log stops growing. Optional pynvml GPU utilization is display-only, never judged. 43 tests.

releases.title: The doctor release
releases.summary: trainproof doctor — zero-config autopsy over a file or a whole directory: auto-discovers logs, triage-sorted summary (failures first), per-log autopsy citing exact numbers. N-way compare table. BREAKING: compare baseline now comes FIRST. No engine or rule changes. 38 tests.

releases.title: Pre-flight: stop a run before it starts
releases.summary: trainproof preflight — deterministic dataset + tokenizer checks before training: malformed JSONL (with line number), empty rows, duplicates, missing eos_token, pad == eos, over-length samples. IO-free engine, lazy tokenizer load, non-zero exit for CI. Completes the lifecycle: preflight · guardian · epoch · compare.

releases.title: The Live Guardian
releases.summary: TrainproofCallback for HF Trainer — one line in your script, re-runs the deterministic rules live. warn by default (never interrupts); opt-in stop_on_fail aborts a doomed run. trainproof watch tails a growing log and exits non-zero on FAIL. Live proof: aborted a diverging Qwen2.5-3B QLoRA (LR 100× too high) at step 20 of 300.

releases.title: Compare engine
releases.summary: trainproof compare <baseline> <run> — ratio rules (loss-floor, end-loss, improvement deficit, grad-norm, baseline sanity) that catch the shuffled-labels run single-run rules can't (6× floor ratio, 3/3 seeds). Total-zero-LR fatality rule from the lr column. EVIDENCE_MATRIX.md: the fault-injection study across 3 seeds (15 real QLoRA runs).

releases.title: The fault-injection gallery
releases.summary: Five real QLoRA runs (Qwen2.5-3B, RTX 5080) — one healthy, four with exactly one knob broken (LR ×100, LR 0, fp16 overflow, shuffled labels) — with unmodified logs shipped in-repo. Dead-run rule. HF/Coqui log adapters. The honest finding: the shuffled-labels run cut loss 62% while learning nothing — indistinguishable from healthy on a single curve.

releases.title: A linter for ML training runs
releases.summary: Deterministic PASS/WARN/FAIL verdicts before you burn GPU time: data preflight, tokenizer coverage, first-epoch verdict (NaN/Inf, divergence, dead runs, grad spikes, LR sanity, throughput). Field test flagged a real 11-hour XTTS fine-tune as diverging — final loss 1.9× above its minimum, reached at 82% of the run. Built on ttsproof.

projects.name: notchecked
projects.tagline: Coverage accounting for validators: what was checked, what could not be checked, and what was never in scope.
projects.description: A schema and accounting layer for tools that check things. Eight terminal coverage states, each carrying who owns the gap and whether it can ever change. Coverage and verdict are enforced as orthogonal axes, so a skipped check can never be reported as a passed one. Reasons come from a vocabulary declared up front rather than free text, counts are derived from the records at read time so a total cannot drift from the rows it summarises, and incomplete coverage never exits zero.
highlights: The same defect found in four unrelated systems - an ML training linter, a directory walk, a compliance report and a retrieval evaluation harness - all rendering absence of evidence as a positive result
Eight terminal states, and a test enforcing that no two share both an owner and a remediation
Coverage and verdict as orthogonal axes: a gap cannot carry a verdict, a checked record cannot carry a skip reason
Two denominators, and only the one computed over mechanically checkable targets is quotable
Hardened by two attacks on its own design before release: five API holes, then 24 realistic cases of which five fit no state at all
Zero dependencies, standard library only, 29 tests, MIT

projects.name: spkproof
projects.description: Pitch trackers fail on rough phonation, and they fail in one direction: octave errors push an estimate up and essentially never down. Pooled with modal speech, that is not noise but differential measurement error, correlated with condition and loaded onto one side of any directional comparison. Four exact tests catch it in a table a study already has. It measures false rejection, not attacks, and it reports problems in the measurement rather than verdicts about any speaker.
highlights: Four exact tests, no approximations: range, octave-harmonic fingerprint, confinement to a condition (Fisher exact), and one-way failures that do not cancel
It found the contamination that made its own author withdraw a published direction: correcting it two equally defensible ways gave opposite answers
Reads a per-utterance table the study already has - no audio, no model refit, no dependencies
A regression test runs it against the published paper's own measurement table and asserts the published numbers, so a change to the library that alters them fails the build
Reports measurement problems, never a judgement about a person - stated in the README because the misuse is obvious and easy

articles.title: My Agent Answers From 0.6% of Its Corpus and Reports It Like a Full Read
articles.dek: My portfolio agent holds 1,003 chunks and answers from six of them — 0.598% — and the answer reads identically to one built from reading all 1,003. That is fine for “he mentions Rust” and false for “he never mentions Rust”, from the same six chunks. Faithfulness cannot catch it: an answer perfectly grounded in what was retrieved can still be wrong about what was not. The control is the shape of the claim, not a coverage threshold.

articles.title: Panagiotis (Panos) Gkilis - Machine Learning Engineer
articles.dek: Production ML systems, MLOps, speech and language AI. A 730M-parameter TTS model trained from scratch and served behind a live API, a grounded RAG agent behind a 32-case adversarial gate, an OpenAI-compatible model gateway, MCP tooling, seven Zenodo DOIs and four open-source libraries. Everything deployed, measured, and open to inspection.

articles.title: A Hundred Per Cent Success Rate and One Usable Answer
articles.dek: I removed the backpressure from my own model gateway to see what would break. Thirty-two callers, thirty-two HTTP 200s, and thirty-one arrived after the caller had given up. Then I made a backend go slow instead of dying, and watched failover log eight successes without ever calling the healthy backend. Both faults produced a clean log.

articles.title: Aether: Real-Time Tracking and Collision Screening in Rust
articles.dek: A two-thousand-line component that turns a live, unreliable sensor feed into a collision picture in under a millisecond per cycle, built to be embedded inside a larger system. What it is, what a system like it is used for, why the problem is hard, and one measured investigation: a fault that caused 16.1% of valid observations to be rejected, cut to 1.9% by an architectural change.

articles.title: Ten Tests, Written Before the Code. The One That Failed Taught Me the Most
articles.dek: I wrote a finite element solver from nothing and pointed it at an answer known since 1898. It landed on 3.00002. Then a test I was sure would pass didn't, two explanations for why both collapsed, and a number the internet repeats confidently failed to reproduce.

articles.title: How Little Your Voice Has to Change Before a Machine Stops Recognising It
articles.dek: Four speakers, eight matched sentences, three encoder architectures. One speaker moved his pitch by less than a semitone and lost a quarter of his identity score. Includes a control that could have killed the result, a prior-art audit that killed my headline claim, and a pre-registered prediction I withdrew because two defensible ways of cleaning the data gave opposite answers.

articles.title: The Canon Is the Database
articles.dek: A fictional universe outgrew my context window. So I stopped treating it as a pile of documents and started treating it as a persistent, machine-readable knowledge system that generation has to be validated against.

articles.title: Geometric Optics Lies: Reproducing a 1976 Black-Hole Calculation from Scratch
articles.dek: The standard shortcut overstates photon emission from a black hole by 4.16x. Six validation gates, two analytic limits the code was never tuned to, and one number I had to retract.

articles.title: Your TTS Model Sounds Great — Until It Says "GPUB"
articles.dek: ttsproof: automated failure-mode QA for text-to-speech, backed by a published 390-sample study.

articles.title: Loss Curves Lie: Building a Deterministic Linter for ML Training Runs
articles.dek: A run learning pure noise reduced its loss by 62% and looked textbook-healthy. trainproof catches the training failures that can be caught — and is honest about the ones that can't.

articles.title: I Use AI to Write My Books. I Wrote the First One by Hand.
articles.dek: Six years, six books, one fantasy world, and a stack of tooling built to stop the machine from drifting. What "AI-assisted" actually looks like when a human directs the whole thing.

articles.title: Six Things Photopea's Scripting API Does That Nobody Wrote Down
articles.dek: Undocumented behaviours in Photopea's Live Messaging API - measured, with the workaround for each. If your automation reports success and changes nothing, one of these is probably why.

articles.title: Why Corrupted Training Data Doesn't Show Up as High Loss
articles.dek: Everyone assumes bad samples announce themselves. Two failures from my own work - one reproducible, one from production - say the opposite: noise is learnable, so it hides.

articles.title: One Integer Deleted the Stop Token From My Loss. The Curve Never Noticed.
articles.dek: My text-to-speech model trained for weeks and never learned to stop talking. The cause was two constants that happened to be equal - and no loss curve, anywhere, could have told me.

articles.title: The Size Where a Model Stops Saying "I Don’t Know"
articles.dek: Five local models, one fact their source text does not contain. Scaling recovered none of it. Compiling the fact worked — above a threshold, with a regression in the middle where the model stopped abstaining and started agreeing.

articles.title: The Same Bug, Four Times, Three of Them Mine
articles.dek: A validator that reports a verdict without reporting its coverage is asserting something it did not measure. I found that in four systems before I admitted it was one problem.
